GM Pays $220 Million To Settle Lawsuit Alleging It Violated Drivers' Privacy For Profit

Good morning! It's Friday, October 30, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift , your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

📌 The Core Development

In this morning's edition, General Motors will pay a $220 million settlement for allegedly violating the privacy of folks who drive its vehicles, Volkswagen is suspending work on the electric Golf because of cost cuts, Aston Martin has now lost $3 billion since Lawrence Stroll took over, and Audi has been promised tariff relief by the Trump administration in order to secure a plant in the U.S.

General Motors is going to pay $220 million to settle allegations that it had illegally collected and sold drivers' private behavior and location data to brokers , who then sold that information to insurers that used it to set and sometimes increase rates. Not a very cool move, if ya ask me. The settlement resolves claims made by 35 U.S. attorneys general over the automaker's Smart Driver program , which enrolled millions of drivers between 2016 and 2024 — when it was discontinued. Other regulators have also been reviewing GM's handling of driver data.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

The automaker was accused of pitching Smart Driver as a program to help people improve their personal driving safety, but GM quickly violated their privacy by reneging on its promise not to sell their data without permission. Many folks who signed up were also enrolled in GM's OnStar safety, navigation and diagnostic service. From Reuters :

The settlement also requires GM to limit driving data it ‌collects, ⁠and obtain drivers' express consent before collecting or sharing that data.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

"Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to ​being clear about what ​information is used, how ⁠it's protected, and the choices customers have about what they share," the spokesperson said.

Insurers such as Allstate, Progressive and Berkshire Hathaway's Geico use so-called telematics in monitoring drivers' habits. They say the ​technology rewards ⁠good driving through lower premiums.
